title: 2023 Saudi Arabian GP: Alonso 5s penalty served with rear jack touching car
text: 2023 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, car 14 (ALO). Alonso received a 5 second time penalty for being out of position on the starting grid. When he served it at his pit stop, the rear jack made contact with the car before the five seconds had elapsed. The stewards added a further 10 second penalty after the race, dropping him from third to fourth; Aston Martin's right-of-review petition succeeded because no prior agreement defined jack contact as 'working on the car', and the podium was restored. The current wording of Article 54.4c) states that touching the car or driver by hand, tools or equipment all constitutes working, so mechanics must not touch the car until the full stationary penalty time has elapsed.

title: 2023 Bahrain GP: Ocon penalty served incorrectly, escalated to 10s
text: 2023 Bahrain Grand Prix, car 31 (OCO). Ocon was given a 5 second time penalty for starting out of position in his grid box. While serving it in the pit stop, his mechanics began working on the car before the 5 seconds had elapsed, so the stewards imposed a 10 second time penalty under Article 54.4e), which supersedes the original penalty. He later collected another 5 second penalty for speeding in the pit lane. Lesson: the stationary hold for a 5s/10s penalty must be fully observed before any tyre change starts, and a breach escalates the penalty.

title: 2024 Austrian GP: Norris 5s penalty for track limits
text: 2024 Austrian Grand Prix, car 4 (NOR). After repeatedly leaving the track at turn 10 (more than three track-limits offences) Norris was handed a 5 second time penalty. A 5s time penalty can either be served at the next pit stop as a stationary hold before work starts, or be added to race time if the driver makes no further stop. Strategists must add the 5.0 s hold to the pit loss when modelling a remaining stop.

title: 2024 Mexico City GP: Verstappen two 10s penalties
text: 2024 Mexico City Grand Prix, car 1 (VER). Verstappen received two separate 10 second time penalties: one for forcing car 4 (NOR) off the track and one for leaving the track and gaining a lasting advantage. Both were served as stationary holds at his single pit stop, where the car could not be touched until it had been stationary for the full 20 seconds, which effectively ended his race result. A 10 second penalty must be modelled as a 10.0 s stationary hold added to the normal pit lane loss.

title: 2019 Canadian GP: Vettel 5s penalty for unsafe rejoin
text: 2019 Canadian Grand Prix, car 5 (VET). Vettel ran wide through the grass at turns 3-4, rejoined the track and forced car 44 (HAM) to take avoiding action. The stewards judged it an unsafe rejoin and gave a 5 second time penalty. Vettel crossed the line first but was classified second because the 5 seconds were added to his race time. A driver leading by less than the penalty margin with no stops remaining loses the position.

title: 2024 Monaco GP: lap-1 red flag gives every car a free tyre change
text: 2024 Monaco Grand Prix. A first-lap crash brought out the red flag. Under Article 57.4b)vii) teams may change wheels and tyres while the race is suspended, so every car switched compounds in the pit lane. Because a red-flag tyre change counts towards the tyre specification requirement of Article 30.5m), most of the field completed the race with no further pit stop. A red flag is the cheapest possible pit window: zero pit-lane time loss.

title: 2024 Sao Paulo GP: red flag tyre change decides the race
text: 2024 Sao Paulo Grand Prix (wet race). Cars 4 (NOR) and 63 (RUS) pitted for fresh intermediates on lap 28 under the VSC. On lap 32 car 43 (COL) crashed and the race was red-flagged. Cars 1 (VER), 31 (OCO) and 10 (GAS), which had not yet stopped, changed to fresh intermediates during the suspension at no time cost under Article 57.4b)vii). They finished 1-2-3; Norris finished 6th. Because intermediates were used, the two dry-compound requirement of Article 30.5m) did not apply. Data: OpenF1 session_key 9636 stints.

title: 2023 Singapore GP: Mercedes double-stack under the VSC
text: 2023 Singapore Grand Prix. On lap 44 car 31 (OCO) stopped on track and the Virtual Safety Car was deployed. Mercedes pitted cars 44 (HAM) and 63 (RUS) from hard to fresh medium tyres under the VSC, where Article 56.4 allows a car to enter the pits for the purpose of changing tyres. The VSC roughly halved their pit-lane time loss compared with a green-flag stop, and they closed down the leaders on the fresher tyres. Car 55 (SAI) stayed out on hards and won from 4 (NOR); Hamilton finished third. Data: OpenF1 session_key 9165 stints.

title: 2024 British GP: intermediate-to-slick crossover timing
text: 2024 British Grand Prix (mixed conditions). Rain arrived around lap 27 and the leaders switched from mediums to intermediates. As the track dried, car 44 (HAM) pitted at the end of lap 38 for soft slicks, one lap before car 4 (NOR), who pitted at the end of lap 39 and lost the lead; car 1 (VER) took hard tyres and finished second. Hamilton won. Because intermediates were used, the two dry-compound rule of Article 30.5m) no longer constrained the final slick choice. Data: OpenF1 session_key 9558 stints.

title: 2021 Abu Dhabi GP: lapped cars and the final-lap safety car restart
text: 2021 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. A late safety car allowed only the lapped cars between the leaders to overtake before the restart, which the subsequent FIA analysis identified as an inconsistent application of the procedure. The regulations were rewritten so that, when the message 'LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE' is shown, all lapped cars must unlap themselves (Article 55.14). Teams that pit for fresh soft tyres under a late safety car gain a large pace advantage at the restart.

title: 2024: Magnussen race ban after reaching 12 penalty points
text: 2024 season, car 20 (MAG). After accumulating 12 penalty points on his Super Licence within a 12-month period (the final points at the 2024 Italian GP), Kevin Magnussen was suspended from the next Competition (the 2024 Azerbaijan GP) and replaced by a reserve driver. Penalty points accompany most time penalties, so repeated aggressive defending carries a suspension risk.

title: Pit entry closed: no stop permitted
text: When Race Control displays 'PIT ENTRY CLOSED' (Article 34.15, typically while a safety car is being deployed and the field is gathered), no car may enter the pit lane except for an emergency. A car that enters a closed pit lane is penalised, normally with a stop-and-go or drive-through. A strategy that schedules a stop on a lap while the pit entry is closed is illegal and must be moved to the first lap after 'PIT ENTRY OPEN' is shown.

title: Pit-lane time loss: green flag vs SC vs VSC
text: Pit-lane time loss is the time a car loses relative to staying on track. Under green flag running it is typically 18-24 s depending on the circuit; OpenF1 measures the raw pit-lane transit (entry line to exit line), and the loss is that transit minus the time the same distance takes at racing speed. Under a safety car the field is slowed to the delta time, so the relative loss drops to roughly 10-14 s; under a VSC every car runs a minimum sector time and the loss is roughly 12-15 s. A pit stop under SC/VSC is therefore a 'cheap stop' worth around 8-10 s of race time.

title: Wet races: the two dry-compound rule no longer applies
text: Article 30.5m) requires two different dry-weather tyre specifications in a dry race. If a driver uses intermediate or wet-weather tyres at any point during the race, the requirement no longer applies, so a car can finish on one dry compound after an intermediate stint. In a fully dry race, finishing without using a second dry specification (for example MEDIUM then MEDIUM) leads to disqualification, unless the race is suspended and not restarted, in which case 30 seconds is added instead.
